hook: The father of geometry, whose textbook was used for 2,000 years.

pages.x: Almost nothing is known about Euclid himself. He taught mathematics in Alexandria around 300 BC, a few years after Alexander the Great founded it, probably at the great Museum and Library set up by its new kings. No real portrait of him exists; every picture is imagined.

He gathered the geometry of the Greeks into one work of 13 books, the Elements. Starting from five simple rules, like "a straight line can be drawn between any two points", he proved 465 results one after another, each resting on those before it.

King Ptolemy I asked whether there was a quicker way to learn geometry than the Elements. Euclid replied: "There is no royal road to geometry." Another story says a student asked what he would gain from it. Euclid told his servant to give the boy a coin, "since he must make a profit from what he learns".
Euclid proved there is no largest prime number: multiply any list of primes and add one, and the result can be divided by none of them.
pages.fx: It is still taught as one of the most beautiful proofs ever found. Today large primes guard every online payment through encryption.

pages.x: The Elements may be the most printed book after the Bible, with over 1,000 editions since 1482. Abraham Lincoln, a young lawyer who wanted to learn what it means to prove something, studied its first six books by candlelight until he could prove their theorems himself.
pages.cap: Abraham Lincoln, who studied Euclid to learn how to argue

pages.x: For more than 2,000 years the Elements was how the world learned mathematics. Its method of proving everything from a few basic rules became the model for mathematics, logic and science.
pts: Wrote the Elements, the most famous maths book ever
Showed how to build proofs from a few basic rules
Proved there are infinitely many prime numbers
